title: Running to the tomb (John 20:1–10)
hook: Peter and the other disciple race; the linen cloths lie folded

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nicodemus came by day with a hundred pounds of myrrh. Your line was in daylight now. How did you let your care be seen? Day six hundred fifty.

In a museum in Paris hangs a painting from 1898 by the Swiss artist Eugène Burnand. There's no tomb in it, no angel, no risen Jesus. Just two men running, at dawn, side by side, hair blown back. One is older, gripping his chest. The younger one leans forward, hands clasped, eyes wide. You can almost hear their breathing. Of all the resurrection scenes he could have painted, Burnand chose the run. And so does John. Before anyone sees anything, two friends run.
screen: `NO TOMB, NO ANGEL. JUST THE RUN.`

segments.voice: It starts with Mary Magdalene. In the King James Bible: "The first day of the week cometh Mary Magdalene early, when it was yet dark, unto the sepulchre, and seeth the stone taken away from the sepulchre." She doesn't think resurrection. She thinks robbery. She runs to Peter and the disciple Jesus loved: "They have taken away the Lord out of the sepulchre, and we know not where they have laid him." And then the race: "So they ran both together: and the other disciple did outrun Peter, and came first to the sepulchre." It's such a human detail. Readers have smiled at it for centuries: the beloved disciple, who many believe is the source behind this Gospel, can't resist mentioning that he won. But he stops at the entrance. He stoops, looks in, sees the linen cloths lying there, and doesn't go in. Peter arrives, out of breath, and walks straight in. He sees the linen cloths, and the cloth that had been around Jesus's head, not with the others, "but wrapped together in a place by itself." That's an odd detail for grave robbers. Thieves don't unwrap a body and leave the wrappings neatly behind. Then the other disciple goes in too, "and he saw, and believed." Believed what, exactly? John adds, honestly, that they didn't yet understand the scripture that he must rise. Something had shifted in him before he understood it. And then, strangely, they both just go home. No announcement. The great news of Easter begins with a race, an empty room, folded cloth, and two men walking home not quite sure what they've seen.
screen: `HE SAW, AND BELIEVED, NOT YET KNOWING.`
then, large: `SO THEY RAN BOTH TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: run to good news. Settle, and breathe. Think about the last time someone told you good news. Did you run toward it, or did you say that's nice and go back to your screen? Now think of someone in your life with good news right now: a new job, a recovery, a baby, a small win. Picture yourself going to them, not walking, running, the way these two ran. If you pray, you can give thanks for their good news. If you don't, simply let yourself be glad for them. The bell holds the time.
Sepulchre. The King James word for the tomb Mary found open at dawn, which Peter and the beloved disciple then ran to see.
Your line: they both ran. Today, when you hear someone's good news, go to them quickly and celebrate it with them, before anything else. Day six hundred fifty.

howItsDone: John 20 is read in many churches on Easter morning, and in some places Christians mark Easter with sunrise services, gathering outdoors before dawn as Mary did.

original.note: Greek: rolled up, wrapped together. the head cloth was lying by itself.

trapdoor: what you thought: two disciples check on a rumor.
what it means: a race at dawn, an empty room, cloths left behind, and belief that comes before understanding.
what a scholar hears: the narrator's little boast that the beloved disciple won, and a head cloth 'rolled up' apart: not what grave robbers would leave.
recall: the world: loved by God, often hostile

notes: Burnand painting (1898), Musée d'Orsay: confirm date, location and the description of the figures (older Peter, younger John).

'Many believe [the beloved disciple] is the source behind this Gospel' (cf. 21:24). Confirm.
Index hook says the linen cloths 'lie folded'; the KJV says 'wrapped together' and the Greek entetyligmenon means rolled up. The script follows the text; Keeper may want to adjust the index hook.
